clue.text: A botched job going uphill, deer shelters you, thank God

indicators.note: the turned deer is a cover with the following letters tucked inside it
in a down entry, travelling uphill means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: an elk is a large deer
U is text-speak for you
DG abbreviates the Latin Deo gratias, 'thanks be to God'

explanation.surface: A climber muddles a job on the way up a hill, sheltering among deer and offering thanks to heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: D.G. is a Latin abbreviation seen on British coins; 'going uphill' reads the deer upwards in this down entry, and 'shelters' wraps it round the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A clumsy improvised fix, thrown together to make something work, is this slang term.

clue.text: I tend lower, lower down not to have a split

annotationWithheld.why: I tend lower, lower down not to have a split (8): NEAT (cattle) + HERD fits 'I tend lower', but no parse of 'lower down not to have a split' gives the letters without a word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: I tend lower, lower down not to have a split

clue.text: Unlike stoic, not reliant on transition

indicators.note: words in transition are changing form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who is no stoic cannot rely on anything during a period of change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on transition' rearranges the ten letters of NOT RELIANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoic endures without complaint; someone impatient and unwilling to put up with things is the opposite.

clue.text: "Nothing universal" badly describes a line in old revamped hit

definitions.text: a line in old revamped hit

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, so it stands for nothing
something universal is found everywhere, i.e. is present all around us

explanation.surface: A slogan of universal nothingness is a poor description of a lyric in an old song that became a hit again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly describes' admits that the title, read cryptically as nil plus everywhere, is only a loose description of 'Nothing universal'. The song was the Troggs' 1967 hit, covered by Wet Wet Wet in 1994.
explanation.definitionFit: The title phrase is the opening line of the Troggs' song, which Wet Wet Wet revived as a long-running number one.

clue.text: God's mounting crisis

indicators.note: in a down entry, mounting means the word climbs, read from bottom to top

parts.note: the Suez Crisis of 1956 was the Anglo-French intervention over the Suez Canal

explanation.surface: A deity faces an escalating emergency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mounting' turns SUEZ upwards. The Suez Crisis was a 1956 British political disaster, so 'crisis' alone can call it to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The king of the Greek gods on Olympus, wielder of thunderbolts.

clue.text: Man — perhaps, no man — is down the plane

parts.note: to bring a plane down is to land it

explanation.surface: Donne's 'no man is an island' is recalled as an aircraft comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is an example of the definition, signalled by 'perhaps'; 'no man' plays on John Donne's line 'No man is an island'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is a piece of land surrounded by sea in the Irish Sea.

clue.text: Stewart is taken by Patrick — who's taking Mickey?

indicators.note: the first pieces are taken into the name that follows, held inside it

parts.note: Pat is short for Patrick
Rod Stewart is the rock singer

explanation.surface: A singer is snapped up by a man named Patrick, and someone is mocking him.
explanation.walkthrough: To take the mickey is British slang for to mock someone; 'taken by' wraps the singer and 'is' inside the short name.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who imitates others mockingly for comic effect is mocking them, the British sense of taking the mickey.

clue.text: Inform uncle, unsure about crossword compiler

indicators.note: being unsure about something means turning it over, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the setter of a crossword refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: Someone tells an uncle, who is puzzled about the person who sets crosswords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unsure about' rearranges UNCLE plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill someone in with information they lack is the phrasal verb here.

clue.text: Old rhymes (when abroad)

parts.note: rhymes collectively are verse
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Ancient nursery rhymes recited while on foreign travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in or going to a foreign country across the sea is the sense shared.

clue.text: Don't start father off on it — I'm way into mine

indicators.note: the word for father is used without its opening letter

parts.note: dad is father
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells a father not to start, while a tunnel speaks up about being a route into a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don't start' strips the opening letter from the word for father; 'off on' simply links it to IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A nearly horizontal passage driven into a hillside gives access to a mine.

clue.text: Spell notice in the way to shelter

annotationWithheld.why: They plot intro for Jerry Springer to avoid the fourth golfer's round (8): J (intro for Jerry) and ELS (golfer) are visible, but no reading of 'Springer to avoid the fourth' gives EZEB
annotationWithheld.clue: They plot intro for Jerry Springer to avoid the fourth golfer's round

clue.text: Not a gentleman long, I'll help ruin Twain's long walk

definitions.text: I'll help ruin Twain's long walk

parts.note: a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably
to be dying for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: An ungentlemanly figure, long in the tooth, confesses to spoiling a stroll that Mark Twain admired.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the saying attributed to Mark Twain that golf is 'a good walk spoiled'; the bag-carrier helps spoil it.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's bag carrier accompanies the player round the course, playing a part in the spoiling of a stroll.

clue.text: On night out it might help secure hot blooded male under arrest

definitions.text: On night out it might help secure

indicators.note: in a down entry, the second piece is placed beneath the first

parts.note: police slang: to collar someone is to arrest them
a stud is a virile, sexually active man

explanation.surface: A passionate man is taken into custody after a night on the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'under' puts STUD below COLLAR in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A small button-like fastener holds a detachable shirt collar in place for a formal evening.

clue.text: Shoot back to get some jazz

indicators.note: going back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: to dart is to shoot or dash quickly

explanation.surface: Someone returns fire, or dashes back, to hear a bit of jazz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses DART.
explanation.definitionFit: Traditional jazz, the New Orleans and Dixieland style, is known by this short form.

clue.text: Painter of internal passageways in urgent need of feeding

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist
venous means relating to veins, the body's internal channels

explanation.surface: An artist who paints the body's inner passages is desperately hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts, so a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremely hungry and craving food is the plain sense.

clue.text: Really light sealing compound

indicators.note: the clue words seal the letters inside them, carrying them within

explanation.surface: A very light material is used to seal joints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sealing' signals the letters are held within REALLY LIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Allyl is an organic chemical group found in compounds such as garlic oil.

clue.text: Place one sense in another sense

indicators.note: the word for the sense is taken in another sense, a word said the same way

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses

explanation.surface: Someone puts one sense inside another, as if mixing faculties.
explanation.walkthrough: SIGHT and SITE are pronounced identically; 'in another sense' signals the change of meaning and spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A location where something is or will be built is a plot of ground.

clue.text: Port Wells passed up — not a word an ace writer embraces

indicators.note: the outer pieces hug the turned initials in their middle

parts.note: shh is an instruction to say not a word
taken as written
A is the abbreviation for an ace in cards
the setter calls themselves I

indicators.note: in a down entry, passed up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: H. G. Wells, the science-fiction writer

explanation.surface: Wells is ignored at a port by a top author who keeps quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer here is H. G. Wells, known by his initials; 'passed up' turns them in this down entry and 'embraces' sets them in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge Chinese city on the Yangtze delta, one of the world's busiest seaports.

clue.text: A person who targeted body in the 30s finally gets time (bird)

parts.words: person who targeted body in the 30s
parts.note: Bill Voce bowled bodyline, aimed at batsmen's bodies, on England's 1932-33 tour

explanation.surface: A cricketer famous for an aggressive 1930s bowling tactic finally gets jail time.
explanation.walkthrough: Bodyline was the England cricket team's 1932-33 tactic of bowling short at the batsman's body; Bill Voce bowled it alongside Harold Larwood.
explanation.definitionFit: A black-and-white wading bird with an upcurved bill, emblem of the RSPB.

clue.text: Short, perhaps, without a bob

parts.note: curt means abrupt or short

indicators.note: the word for perhaps loses the letter named next

parts.note: say can mean perhaps, as in 'about, say, ten'

explanation.surface: A short haircut, perhaps one with no bob style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes A from SAY, leaving SY. 'bob' looks like a haircut but is the definition, a little bending of the knees.
explanation.definitionFit: A bob is a quick bending of the knee in respect, especially by a woman.

clue.text: A wine valley is 9 foot 2 short to begin with

parts.note: the Napa Valley is California's wine region
9 across means abroad; French for 'is' is est

explanation.surface: A Californian wine valley supposedly stretches nine feet, two of them short at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: '9' points to 9 across, OVERSEAS, so 'is 9' is 'is' in a foreign tongue: French EST. The definition means a metrical foot of two short syllables then a long one.
explanation.definitionFit: A metrical unit of verse made of two unstressed syllables followed by a stressed syllable.

clue.text: Tango in 3-D raising little emotion

indicators.note: the letter is placed inside the word for 3-D

parts.note: a solid shape has three dimensions
T is Tango in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Dancing a tango in three dimensions stirs hardly any feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts T inside SOLID.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone impassive and showing little feeling is dull and unemotional.

clue.text: Union getting drunk carousing — not tasteful or elegant

indicators.note: letters that get drunk reel about, so these are scrambled

explanation.surface: A trade union drinks heavily while carousing, without class or grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting drunk' rearranges CAROUSING after U.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking grace and courtesy is the old sense, as well as rude.

clue.text: Getting indoors, I pass wind

indicators.note: the letter gets inside the mountain-pass word, enclosed by it

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

explanation.surface: Someone heading indoors breaks wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting indoors' puts I inside COL. 'wind' is the verb to twist, not air.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind something is to wrap it round in loops, the verb sense.

clue.text: Blunder — no longer fancy female moving out

indicators.note: the letter for female moves out of the phrase, leaving it

parts.note: to go off someone is to stop fancying them

explanation.surface: A mistake: someone goes off a woman who moves out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving out' removes one F from GO OFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A silly mistake is the slang noun and also the verb.

clue.text: What in Fawlty Towers it has to turn on?

definitions.text: What in Fawlty Towers it has to turn on?

parts.note: Manuel, the Spanish waiter in Fawlty Towers, keeps saying 'Que?', Spanish for what

indicators.note: the contraction is turned to read backwards

parts.note: it's is short for it has
taken as written

explanation.surface: What does the plot of Fawlty Towers hinge upon?
explanation.walkthrough: Fawlty Towers is a 1970s British sitcom. 'to turn' reverses ITS to STI. The whole clue is itself an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentence ending in a query mark, like the clue itself, asks something.

clue.text: Quick turn gets queen a heavenly inspiration

parts.note: a U-turn is an abrupt turn
a rani is a Hindu queen

explanation.surface: A queen makes a sudden about-face to find celestial inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muse of astronomy in Greek myth, who inspired study of the heavens.
